Juvenile Mango tilapia (Sarotherodon galilaeus) hatch from demersal, adhesive eggs that measure between 1.7 and 2.6 mm in diameter. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarvae possess a prominent yolk sac and carry an extremely modest wet weight at birth of 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the small size of the chorionate embryo and is a common trait among cichlid species that engage in biparental oral incubation. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching, and the depletion of these nutrients triggers the onset of exogenous feeding once the mouth gape achieves functional opening. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of tropical lacustrine habitats (30 °C [T = 30 °C]), the endangered young pass through the exotrophic transition rapidly and begin actively foraging on microcrustaceans. The rapid growth that follows is fueled by high ingestion rates, and individuals quickly progress from the prolarva to the fingerling stage within a span of weeks. This early developmental trajectory is critically dependent on water temperature, and deviations from 30 °C can substantially alter the timing of the trophic switch and subsequent survival.

As the fingerlings transition into the juvenile stage, they exhibit a pronounced acceleration in somatic growth that is modulated by both food availability and ambient temperature. At a constant water temperature of 30 °C, the species attains sexual maturation at a total length at puberty of 16.3 cm [Lp = 16.3 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 77 grams [Wwp = approximately 77 grams] based on the length-weight relationship derived from field-caught specimens. This size threshold marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence, during which the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated. The body mass accumulated during the juvenile period is substantial, and the shift from somatic investment toward reproductive physiology occurs once individuals cross this length-based maturation boundary. Comparative data from related tilapiine cichlids suggest that a total length at puberty of 16.3 cm is relatively moderate, placing Sarotherodon galilaeus in an intermediate position among its congeners. The attainment of this size is heavily influenced by local ecological conditions, and individuals reared under suboptimal thermal regimes or low food rations may experience significant delays in the timing of reproductive activation.

Once individuals surpass the maturation threshold, they enter the sexually mature adult stage and begin investing resources into reproductive effort. Spawning adult females produce multiple clutches across an extended breeding season, and the maximum reproductive output of the species has been quantified under controlled conditions. Females produce one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch] and can complete up to six to seven clutches annually [F_R_i = up to six to seven clutches annually] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 30 °C, yielding a substantial annual fecundity. The gamete release associated with each spawning event is preceded by a period of nest construction and courtship behavior typical of substrate-spawning cichlids. Gravid individuals display conspicuous coloration changes that signal reproductive readiness to potential mates. Following the fertilization and subsequent oral incubation of the fertilised ova, the female broods the yolk-laden eggs for a period of approximately two weeks before the hatching event takes place. The reproductive strategy of this species is thus characterized by frequent, low-fecundity spawning events coupled with intensive parental care, a combination that enhances offspring survival in the variable environments of West African freshwater systems.

The ultimate wet weight that a fully grown Mango tilapia can achieve is approximately 1,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,100 grams], a value derived from the asymptotic length estimate of 39.5 cm [Li = 39.5 cm] for ultimate total length using the species-specific length-weight conversion formula. This maximum recorded body mass in adults is attained only after several years of sustained growth, and relatively few individuals in natural populations reach this upper size limit due to the combined pressures of predation, fishing mortality, and seasonal resource limitation. The largest specimens are typically dominant nest-guarding adults that occupy the most productive foraging territories and thus maintain elevated feeding rates throughout their lives. Sarotherodon galilaeus reaches an ultimate total length of 39.5 cm [Li = 39.5 cm], a moderate size among tilapiine cichlids that exhibits moderate inter-population variation depending on local environmental conditions and fishing pressure. In habitats where food resources are abundant and competition is low, individuals may approach or even slightly exceed this asymptotic size, although the growth rate decelerates markedly once the fish approach their final adult dimensions. The corresponding ultimate body mass of 1,100 grams is consistent with the general cichlid pattern of indeterminate growth.

In terms of longevity, the oldest documented individual of Sarotherodon galilaeus reached a maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] under seminatural captive conditions at 30 °C, suggesting that senescence typically occurs gradually in this iteroparous cichlid at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. This lifespan of 11 years is notable for a fish of its body size, as many comparably sized cichlids in tropical freshwaters exhibit shorter natural longevities, often not exceeding eight years. The completion of the lifespan in older individuals is marked by progressive physiological deterioration, including reduced feeding efficiency, diminished gonadal output, and increased susceptibility to parasitic infections. Post-reproductive mortality rates rise sharply after the age of ten years, and senescent adult death is rarely observed in wild populations because extrinsic mortality factors typically intervene before the fish reaches its physiological maximum age. The combination of a moderate adult body size, a reproductive strategy centered on repeated spawning events, and a relatively extended natural lifespan positions Sarotherodon galilaeus as a species with a comparatively slow life-history pace for a tropical cichlid, a pattern that has important implications for its population dynamics and sustainable fishery management.
